Meta.name: ArchLab
Meta.title: ArchLab: practise AWS architecture design for SAA-C03
Meta.description: An AWS architecture lab: assemble designs by drag and drop, simulate load and incidents, tune for cost. Prepare for AWS Solutions Architect Associate (SAA-C03).

Fields.auto_scaling_hint: Target tracking ~60% CPU; new instances take ~2 ticks to boot.
Fields.multi_az_rds_hint: Synchronous standby in another AZ with automatic failover. Costs ×2, serves no reads.
Fields.multi_az_cache_hint: A replica in another AZ takes over when the primary dies. Costs ×2.
Fields.provisioned_lambda_hint: Keeps environments warm to avoid cold starts. +$15/month.
Fields.provisioned_dynamodb_hint: Pay a fixed price for RCU/WCU, cheaper for steady traffic. Off = on-demand, pay per request.
Fields.cache_api_hint: CloudFront caches ~50% of dynamic reads at the edge.
Fields.encrypted_hint: Turn it on at creation. For an existing RDS: snapshot → encrypted copy → restore.

users.desc: Your users. Every request starts here.
users.tip: "Users around the world" usually points to CloudFront, Global Accelerator or Route 53 latency routing.

route53.desc: AWS DNS. Routes by latency, runs health checks and fails over to a standby Region.
route53.tip: Failover routing + health checks for active-passive DR; latency routing for global users; Alias records for the zone apex.

globalAccelerator.desc: Two static anycast IPs that bring traffic onto the AWS backbone near users. Cuts far-user latency by ~50%.
globalAccelerator.tip: Pick Global Accelerator for static IPs, non-HTTP TCP/UDP, or fast cross-Region failover. Pick CloudFront for cacheable content.

waf.desc: Web Application Firewall: blocks ~98% of bot and attack traffic before it reaches servers.
waf.tip: WAF attaches to CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway and AppSync. Rate-based rules stop floods; Shield Advanced adds layer 3/4 DDoS protection and the SRT team.

cloudfront.desc: CDN with 400+ edge locations. Serves ~95% of static files from the edge, cutting origin load and latency.
cloudfront.tip: S3 + CloudFront with OAC is the textbook answer for static websites. Use signed URLs or cookies for paid content.

alb.desc: Application Load Balancer: spreads HTTP requests across servers in many AZs and skips unhealthy ones.
alb.tip: ALB: layer 7, path and host routing. NLB: layer 4, static IPs, ultra low latency. GWLB: third-party security appliances.

apiGateway.desc: Managed front door for REST, HTTP and WebSocket APIs, usually in front of Lambda. Pay per request.
apiGateway.tip: Throttling, usage plans with API keys, caching, 29-second integration timeout.

ec2.desc: Virtual servers that run your code. Set size, copies, AZ, pricing and Auto Scaling.
ec2.tip: Stateless instances in a multi-AZ ASG behind an ALB is the classic HA pattern. Spot for interruptible work, Reserved or Savings Plans for steady base load.

lambda.desc: Runs code without servers, scales to about 1,000 concurrent requests, billed per request.
lambda.tip: Up to 15 minutes and 10 GB of memory. Cold starts → provisioned concurrency. More expensive than EC2 for high, steady traffic.

elasticache.desc: In-memory cache (Redis/Valkey/Memcached). Answers ~85% of reads in 1–2 ms; the database only sees misses.
elasticache.tip: Store sessions to keep servers stateless. Redis has replicas, Multi-AZ and persistence; Memcached is simple, multi-threaded and has no replicas.

rds.desc: Managed relational database (MySQL, PostgreSQL…). A write costs 3× a read.
rds.tip: Multi-AZ = high availability (the standby serves no reads). Read replicas = read scaling, can be cross-Region. RDS Proxy for many Lambda connections.

aurora.desc: AWS MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible database: 6 copies across 3 AZs, faster than RDS, survives an AZ loss on its own.
aurora.tip: Aurora Global Database for cross-Region DR (RPO about 1 second), up to 15 Aurora Replicas, Serverless v2 for spiky load.

readReplica.desc: Read-only, asynchronous copy of RDS. Takes reads, never writes.
readReplica.tip: Read replicas scale reads and reporting and can be promoted during DR. Do not confuse them with the Multi-AZ standby.

dynamodb.desc: Serverless key-value NoSQL with single-digit ms latency, replicated across 3 AZs.
dynamodb.tip: On-demand for unpredictable traffic, provisioned with auto scaling for steady traffic. DAX for microsecond caching, Global Tables for multi-Region.

s3.desc: Virtually unlimited object storage with 11 nines of durability. Holds images, video and static files.
s3.tip: Storage classes and lifecycle rules to save money; versioning and replication for DR; presigned URLs for temporary uploads and downloads.

sqs.desc: Managed queue. Accepts work instantly so users never wait, and lets workers process it at their own pace.
sqs.tip: Decouple and smooth spikes. Standard: at-least-once; FIFO: ordered, exactly-once. DLQ for failing messages. Scale an ASG on queue depth.

sns.desc: Pub/sub: one message is pushed to many subscribers at once (fan-out).
sns.tip: SNS → many SQS queues is the classic fan-out pattern. Use message filtering so each queue gets only the events it needs.

azOutage.name: AZ outage
azOutage.heads_up: Mid-round, AZ "a" may lose power. Anything that lives only there goes down with it.
azOutage.page: 5xx errors spike and the us-east-1a dashboard turns red.

regionOutage.name: Region outage
regionOutage.heads_up: Word is {region} is about to have a long, major outage.

spotInterruption.name: Spot interruption
spotInterruption.heads_up: AWS can take Spot capacity back with only a 2-minute notice.
spotInterruption.page: Spot instances got their interruption notice and shut down.

flashSale.name: Flash sale
flashSale.heads_up: Marketing scheduled a flash sale: traffic triples for a short while.
flashSale.page: Traffic is surging and checkout is getting slow.

ddos.name: Bot attack
ddos.heads_up: A botnet is eyeing your API.
ddos.page: Strange requests jump 6×, server CPU is pegged.

cacheCrash.name: Cache crash
cacheCrash.heads_up: The cache node may die suddenly at peak time.
cacheCrash.page: The cache stopped answering; every read hits the database.

viral.name: Going viral
viral.heads_up: Your post is spreading: traffic keeps climbing up to 4×.

encryptData.title: Encrypt data
encryptData.desc: Every data store (DB, cache, S3, SQS) must have encryption at rest (KMS).

privateData.title: Private databases
privateData.desc: Only servers (EC2/Lambda) may connect to databases and caches.

noPublicServers.title: No public servers
noPublicServers.desc: EC2 must sit behind an ALB, CloudFront or API Gateway.

fanOut.title: Fan-out
fanOut.desc: Every event must reach at least 2 systems through SNS → SQS → worker.

drainQueue.title: Drain the queue
drainQueue.desc: At the end of the round, no more than 5% of the work is still queued.

Issues.users_unconnected: Users are not linked to anything: pull a wire from the Users box to a component.
Issues.loop: There is a loop at {name}: requests go round in circles.
Issues.nowhere_read: {name} receives read requests but has no data source: link it to a database or cache.
Issues.nowhere_write: {name} receives write requests but nowhere to store them: link it to a database.
Issues.nowhere_static: {name} receives file downloads but has no file store: link it to S3 or a server.
Issues.nowhere_job: {name} receives background jobs but nothing can run them.
Issues.alb_target: {name} only sends requests to servers (EC2/Lambda), not straight to databases.
Issues.no_balancer: {name} has several instances but no ALB in front, so every request lands on one of them: put an ALB before the EC2 group.
Issues.replica_write: {name}: a read replica is read-only; writes must go to the primary database.
Issues.data_split: Writes are split across databases that do not sync (like {name}): link the primary database to its copy (e.g. RDS → RDS, Aurora → Aurora, DynamoDB → DynamoDB) to replicate the data.
Issues.stale_data: {name} left replication during failover and misses the writes made during the incident, yet the app still uses it: link the servers to the new primary, or use Aurora Global Database so the old primary rejoins as a copy.
Issues.queue_no_consumer: Nobody consumes {name}: connect the queue to EC2 or Lambda.
Issues.down: {name} failed during the incident and nothing replaced it.
Issues.overloaded: {name} is past its capacity and rejects requests: scale it up, scale it out or offload it.
Issues.public_data: {name} is exposed: only servers may talk to databases.
Issues.public_server: {name} takes traffic straight from the internet: put an ALB, CloudFront or API Gateway in front.
Issues.no_fan_out: You need SNS sending to at least 2 SQS queues, each with a worker.
Issues.backlog: Queue {name} still has a backlog: add workers or bigger ones.
Issues.slow: Average response time is over target; {name} adds the most delay.
Issues.cold_start: {name} hits cold starts when traffic jumps: turn on provisioned concurrency.
Issues.over_budget: Over budget: {name} costs the most. Find a cheaper option.

Result.cheaper: Met! Cut the cost further for three stars.

Intro.audience: Users by closest Region: {split}. Serving users from another Region adds ~150 ms unless the edge answers.

HowToPlayPage.title: Guide
HowToPlayPage.intro: Each stage is a business requirement: traffic, budget, latency and sometimes an incident. Assemble an AWS architecture, run the simulation and tune it until it meets the bar.

draw.title: Assemble the architecture
draw.items:
Place AWS services from the Components panel onto the canvas (a single click drops one in the middle).
Link two boxes by pulling a wire from a handle on one box to the other.
Select a box to set its size, instance count, AZ, pricing, Multi-AZ, encryption and Region.
Drag the background to pan; hold Ctrl and scroll to zoom.

run.title: Run the simulation
run.items:
A stage is met when at least 99% of requests are served, average latency is within target, monthly cost fits the budget and every rule is satisfied.
The colour bar under each box is its load: green is fine, orange is near the limit, red is over capacity.
The briefing names the expected incident; when it happens you only see symptoms and have to work out the cause.
The cheapest design that still meets the bar earns three stars.

aws.title: More AWS aspects
aws.items:
Multi-AZ and multi-Region: place instances in AZ a/b, RDS Multi-AZ, Route 53 failover to another Region.
Target-tracking Auto Scaling; new instances take ~2 ticks to boot.
Pricing: On-Demand, Reserved (−40%), Spot (−70% but can be interrupted).
Pay-per-request serverless: Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB on-demand. Cheap at low traffic, pricey at high traffic.
Security: WAF, KMS encryption, databases reachable only from servers, servers behind an ALB, CloudFront or API Gateway.
Users served from a Region far from them pay ~150 ms extra unless served at the edge.

fail.title: Read the results and improve
fail.items:
The component at fault is circled in red with an explanation.
"Run details" shows a timeline chart and the cost of each component.
Need help? Hints come in two steps: a pointer, then the reference design (the stage then caps at two stars).

study.title: Study for SAA-C03
study.items:
Every round links to lessons that explain the services and how the exam asks about them.
Practice: English scenario questions with explanations, plus a 65-question, 130-minute mock exam.
Flashcards for quick review of numbers and concepts.

shortcuts.title: Keyboard shortcuts

shortcuts.delete: Delete / Backspace: remove the selected box or wire.
